newsitem.title: EGYPT: Suez Canal hawks deals to lure traffic in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Suez Canal hawks deals to lure traffic in 1997.

text.p: The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) announced on Sunday a package of bargains it hopes will lure traffic away from alternative routes and back to the strategic waterway that links the Red Sea and Mediterranean.

Speaking to reporters at SCA headquarters in Ismailiya, Chairman Ahmed Fadel also said that transit dues for all types of ships travelling through the Suez Canal would remain unchanged for 1997, adding that the measures were aimed at providing a thriftier option to going round the Cape.

"Rates have been the same from 1994 to 1996 and for 1997 there will be no change considering the economics of operating and to encourage them (ships) to use the canal instead of making the trip round Good Hope," Fadel said.
Facing stiff competition from the Cape of Good Hope route and the SUMED pipeline, which pumps oil between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean, Suez Canal revenues have been on the slide.
The SCA's statistics department said on Friday revenues for the first 10 months of 1996 fell to $1.481 billion from $1.606 billion in the same period last year.

Fadel told a news conference that the SCA's aim was to boost income -- a main source of foreign currency for Egypt -- and that he hoped the new tolls, bargain deals and a more personal approach would help.

"We have tried to increase the income of the Suez Canal. We also take care to be in direct contact with ship owners for them to come through. We met with a big number of representatives and shippers -- direct contact is very important," Fadel said.
He dismissed SUMED as competition, saying that although the pipeline was pumping about 117 million tonnes of crude a year, it was servicing different customers.

"Ships discharging at SUMED cannot pass through the canal. All ships that go to Ein el-Sukhana (the Red Sea terminal) are over the capacity of the Suez but the ships which call at Sidi Kirir (Mediterranean terminal) can pass.
"If we say that they (SUMED) have taken business out of Suez Canal I don't think this is true. Actually we are trying to achieve a mutual benefit to all involved," he said.

Fadel said the SCA was also holding talks with Jordan to increase traffic between the canal and the Red Sea port of Aqaba. The SCA also listed the following special offers to crude tankers, liquefied natural gas tankers and container ships:
CRUDE TANKERS
-- Clients that take between one and two million tonnes of crude through the canal during 1997 will be eligible for a five percent discount, both loaded and in ballast.
-- Clients that take between two and three million tonnes of crude through the canal during 1997 will be eligible for a 10 percent discount.
-- Clients that take through more than three million tonnes of crude in 1997 get a 30 percent discount.
-- The maximum toll for a round trip by any tanker, loaded or in ballast, is 330,000 special drawing rights (SDRs) (about $475,000), regardless of the tanker's net tonnage.
-- The SCA also said it was willing to negotiate special deals for firms that want to transport any quantity of crude from the Gulf through the canal in 1997.
LNG TANKERS
-- Loaded northbound tankers are eligible for a 35 percent discount regardless of destination and the same discount is to be granted to the ship upon its ballast southbound trip.
-- Loaded southbound tankers are eligible for a 25 percent discount under the same terms.
CONTAINER SHIPS
-- The SCA cut rates for ships with net tonnages over 70,000 to 1.38 SDRs per tonne from 2.42 SDRs a tonne when loaded. It also cut ballast rates to 1.56 SDRs a tonne from 2.06 SDRs.
-- Containers are also to be exempt from extra dues if the top tier contains no more than 10 containers and if the top tier does not protrude more than four feet.
(one SDR=$1.44)
